#7211. Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (236 w)

Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (236 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add fresh properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones. On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.

Breaking: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (205 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.27895v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I have a lot of respect for iOS/Mac developers.
  • I believe that ML is a newly introduced way to build software, and I know that many Swift developers want to incorporate AI features in their apps.
  • However, using an LLM model such as Llama in an app involves several tasks which many people face and solve alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I have a lot of respect for iOS/Mac developers. I started writing apps for iPhones in 2007, when not even APIs or documentation existed. The latest devices adopted some unfamiliar decisions in the constraint space, with a combination of power, screen real estate, UI idioms, network access, persistence, and latency that was different to what we were used to before. Yet, this community soon managed to create top-notch applications that felt at home with the new paradigm.

I believe that ML is a newly introduced way to build software, and I know that many Swift developers want to incorporate AI features in their apps. The ML ecosystem has matured a lot, with thousands of models that solve a wide variety of problems. Moreover, LLMs have recently emerged as almost general-purpose tools – they can be adapted to new domains as long as we can model our task to work on text or text-like data. We are witnessing a defining moment in computing history, where LLMs are going out of research labs and becoming computing tools for everybody.

However, using an LLM model such as Llama in an app involves several tasks which many people face and solve alone. We have been exploring this space and would love to continue working on it with the community. We aim to create a set of tools and building blocks that help developers build faster.

Today, we are publishing this guide to go through the steps required to run a model such as Llama 2 on your Mac using Core ML. We are also releasing alpha libraries and tools to support developers in the journey. We are calling all Swift developers interested in ML – is that all Swift developers? – to contribute with PRs, bug reports, or opinions to improve this together.

Video: Llama 2 (7B) chat model running on an M1 MacBook Pro with Core ML.

It has been revealed that when I published tweets showing Falcon or Llama 2 running on my Mac, I got many questions from other developers asking how to convert those models to Core ML, because they want to use them in their apps as well. Conversion is a crucial step, but it's just the first piece of the puzzle. The real reason I write those apps is to face the same problems that any other developer would and identify areas where we can help. We'll go through some of these tasks in the rest of this post, explaining where (and where not) we have tools to help.

According to recent reports, core ML is Apple's native framework for Machine Learning, and also the name of the file format it uses. After you convert a model from (for example) PyTorch to Core ML, you can use it in your Swift apps. The Core ML framework automatically selects the best hardware to run your model on: the CPU, the GPU, or a specialized tensor unit called the Neural Engine. A combination of several of these compute units is also possible, depending on the characteristics of your system and the model details.

Sources indicate that to see what it looks like to convert a model in real life, we'll look at converting the recently-released Llama 2 model. The process can sometimes be convoluted, but we offer some tools to help. These tools won't always work, as newly introduced models are being introduced all the time, and we need to make adjustments and modifications.

This is an automated tool built on top of exporters (see below) that either works for your model, or doesn't. It requires no coding: enter the Hub model identifier, select the task you blueprint to use the model for, and click apply. If the conversion succeeds, you can push the converted Core ML weights to the Hub, and you are done!

You can visit the Space or use it directly here:.

Sources indicate that this library gives you a lot more options to configure the conversion task. In addition, it lets you create your own conversion configuration class, which you may use for additional control or to work around conversion problems.

In a recent development, this is the lowest-level approach and therefore provides maximum control. It can still fail for some models (especially new ones), but you always have the option to dive inside the source code and try to figure out why.

According to recent reports, the good news about Llama 2 is that we did the legwork and the conversion process works using any of these methods. The bad news is that it failed to convert when it was released, and we had to do some fixing to support it. We briefly look at what happened in the appendix so you can get a taste of what to do when things go wrong.

According to recent reports, I've followed the conversion process for some recent models (Llama 2, Falcon, StarCoder), and I've applied what I learned to both exporters and the transformers-to-coreml Space. This is a summary of some takeaways:.

We'll keep adding best practices to our tools so you don't have to discover the same issues again.

There's no point in converting models if they don't run fast on your target hardware and respect system resources. The models mentioned in this post are pretty massive for local use, and we are consciously using them to stretch the limits of what's possible with current technology and understand where the bottlenecks are.

For production applications, consider iterating with smaller models, especially during development, and then apply optimization techniques to select the smallest model you can afford for your use case.

In a recent development, swift-transformers is an in-progress Swift package that aims to provide a transformers-like API to Swift developers. Let's see what it has and what's missing.

According to recent reports, tokenization solves two complementary tasks: adapt text input to the tensor format used by the model and convert results from the model back to text. The process is nuanced, for example:.

In a recent development, there are a few general tokenization algorithms, and a lot of different normalization and pre-processing steps that are crucial to using the model effectively. The transformers library made the decision to abstract all those operations in the same library (tokenizers), and represent the decisions as configuration files that are stored in the Hub alongside the model. For example, this is an excerpt from the configuration of the Llama 2 tokenizer that describes just the normalization step:.

Sources indicate that it reads like this: normalization is a sequence of operations applied in order. First, we Prepend character _ to the input string. Then we replace all spaces with _. There's a huge list of potential operations, they can be applied to regular expression matches, and they have to be performed in a very specific order. The code in the tokenizers library takes care of all these details for all the models in the Hub.

In contrast, projects that use language models in other domains, such as Swift apps, usually resort to hardcoding these decisions as part of the app's source code. This is fine for a couple of models, but then it's difficult to replace a model with a different one, and it's easy to make mistakes.

What we are doing in swift-transformers is replicate those abstractions in Swift, so we write them once and everybody can use them in their apps. We are just getting started, so coverage is still small. Feel free to open issues in the repo or contribute your own!

Recent findings suggest that specifically, we right now support BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding) tokenizers, one of the three main families in use today. The GPT models, Falcon and Llama, all use this method. Support for Unigram and WordPiece tokenizers will come later. We haven't ported all the possible normalizers, pre-tokenizers and post-processors - just the ones we encountered during our conversions of Llama 2, Falcon and GPT models.

This is how to use the Tokenizers module in Swift:.

However, you don't usually need to tokenize the input text yourself - the Generation code will take care of it.

According to recent reports, as explained above, transformers heavily use configuration files stored in the Hub. We prepared a simple Hub module to download configuration files from the Hub, which is used to instantiate the tokenizer and retrieve metadata about the model.

According to recent reports, regarding models, we created a simple LanguageModel type as a wrapper for a Core ML model, focusing on the text generation task. Using protocols, we can query any model with the same API.

Industry observers note that to retrieve the appropriate metadata for the model you use, swift-transformers relies on a few custom metadata fields that must be added to the Core ML file when converting it. swift-transformers will use this information to download all the necessary configuration files from the Hub. These are the fields we use, as presented in Xcode's model preview:.

Sources indicate that exporters and transformers-to-coreml will automatically add these fields for you. Please, make sure you add them yourself if you use coremltools manually.

Recent findings suggest that language models are trained to predict a probability distribution of the next token that may appear as a continuation to an input sequence. In order to compose a response, we need to call the model multiple times until it produces a special termination token, or we reach the length we desire. There are many ways to decide what's the next best token to use. We right now support two of them:.

Recent findings suggest that additional methods such as "nucleus sampling" will come later. We recommend this blog post (updated recently) for an excellent overview of generation methods and how they work. Sophisticated methods such as assisted generation can also be very useful for optimization!

Industry observers note that so far, we've tested swift-transformers with a handful of models to validate the main design decisions. We are looking forward to trying many more!

swift-chat is a simple demo app built on swift-transformers. Its main purpose is to show how to use swift-transformers in your code, but it can also be used as a model tester tool.

Recent findings suggest that to use it, download a Core ML model from the Hub or create your own, and select it from the UI. All the relevant model configuration files will be downloaded from the Hub, using the metadata information to identify what model type this is.

The first time you load a new model, it will take some time to prepare it. In this phase, the CoreML framework will compile the model and decide what compute devices to run it on, based on your machine specs and the model's structure. This information is cached and reused in future runs.

Sources indicate that the app is intentionally simple to make it readable and concise. It also lacks a few features, primarily because of the current limitations in model context size. For example, it does not have any provision for "system prompts", which are useful for specifying the behaviour of your language model and even its personality.

It has been revealed that we introduced a set of tools to help Swift developers incorporate language models in their apps. I can't wait to see what you create with them, and I look forward to improving them with the community's help! Don't hesitate to get in touch :).

You can safely ignore this section unless you've experienced Core ML conversion problems and are ready to fight :).

In my experience, there are two frequent reasons why PyTorch models fail to convert to Core ML using coremltools:.

PyTorch has a lot of operations, and all of them have to be mapped to an intermediate representation (MIL, for Model Intermediate Language), which in turn is converted to native Core ML instructions. The set of PyTorch operations is not static, so fresh ones have to be added to coremltools too. In addition, some operations are really complex and can work on exotic combinations of their arguments. An example of a recently-added, very complex op, was scaled dot-product attention, introduced in PyTorch 2. An example of a partially supported op is einsum: not all possible equations are translated to MIL.

Even for supported PyTorch operations, it's very difficult to ensure that the translation process works on all possible inputs across all the different input types. Keep in mind that a single PyTorch op can have multiple backend implementations for different devices (cpu, CUDA), input types (integer, float), or precision (float16, float32). The product of all combinations is staggering, and sometimes the way a model uses PyTorch code triggers a translation path that may have not been considered or tested.

This is what happened when I first tried to convert Llama 2 using coremltools:.

By comparing different versions of transformers, I could see the problem started happening when this line of code was introduced. It's part of a recent transformers refactor to better deal with causal masks in all models that use them, so this would be a massive problem for other models, not just Llama.

In a recent development, what the error screenshot is telling us is that there's a type mismatch trying to fill the mask tensor. It comes from the 0 in the line: it's interpreted as an int, but the tensor to be filled contains floats, and using different types was rejected by the translation process. In this particular case, I came up with a patch for coremltools, but fortunately this is rarely necessary. In many cases, you can patch your code (a 0.0 in a local copy of transformers would have worked), or create a "special operation" to deal with the exceptional case. Our exporters library has very good support for custom, special operations. See this example for a missing einsum equation, or this one for a workaround to make StarCoder models work until a latest version of coremltools is released.

Fortunately, coremltools coverage for newly introduced operations is good and the team reacts very fast.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

Breaking: Beyond Visual Fidelity: Comparing Categorical and Continuous World Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (188 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27870v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.

Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (252 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27860v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed. Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become the de facto last training step of LLMs such as GPT-4 or Claude to ensure that the language model's outputs are aligned with human expectations such as chattiness or safety features. However, it brings some of the complexity of RL into NLP: we need to build a good reward function, train the model to estimate the value of a state, and at the same time be careful not to strive too far from the original model and produce gibberish instead of sensible text. Such a process is quite involved requiring a number of complex moving parts where it is not always easy to get things right.

Sources indicate that the recent paper Direct Preference Optimization by Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell et al. proposes to cast the RL-based objective used by existing methods to an objective which can be directly optimized via a simple binary cross-entropy loss which simplifies this process of refining LLMs greatly.

This blog-post introduces the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) method which is now available in the TRL library and shows how one can fine tune the recent Llama v2 7B-parameter model on the stack-exchange preference dataset which contains ranked answers to questions on the various stack-exchange portals.

In a recent development, in the traditional model of optimising human derived preferences via RL, the goto method has been to use an auxiliary reward model and fine-tune the model of interest so that it maximizes this given reward via the machinery of RL. Intuitively we use the reward model to provide feedback to the model we are optimising so that it generates high-reward samples more often and low-reward samples less often. At the same time we use a frozen reference model to make sure that whatever is generated does not deviate too much and continues to maintain generation diversity. This is typically done by adding a KL penalty to the full reward maximisation objective via a reference model, which serves to prevent the model from learning to cheat or exploit the reward model.

The DPO formulation bypasses the reward modeling step and directly optimises the language model on preference data via a key insight: namely an analytical mapping from the reward function to the optimal RL policy that enables the authors to transform the RL loss over the reward and reference models to a loss over the reference model directly! This mapping intuitively measures how well a given reward function aligns with the given preference data. DPO thus starts with the optimal solution to the RLHF loss and via a change of variables derives a loss over only the reference model!

Thus this direct likelihood objective can be optimized without the need for a reward model or the need to perform the potentially fiddly RL based optimisation.

The TRL library comes with helpers for all these parts, however the DPO training does away with the task of reward modeling and RL (steps 3 and 4) and directly optimizes the DPO object on preference annotated data.

In this respect we would still need to do the step 1, but instead of steps 3 and 4 we need to provide the DPOTrainer in TRL with preference data from step 2 which has a very specific format, namely a dictionary with the following three keys:.

Once we have the dataset sorted the DPO loss is essentially a supervised loss which obtains an implicit reward via a reference model and thus at a high-level the DPOTrainer requires the base model we wish to optimize as well as a reference model:.

This controls how much we pay attention to the reference model in the sense that as beta gets smaller the more we ignore the reference model. In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27826v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.

arXiv:2611.27811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27808v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local-patch methods offer a communication-efficient alternative to Distributed Data Parallelism ($\mathtt{DDP}$), but introduce additional hyperparameters that require costly tuning. For $\mathtt{DDP}$, zero-shot hyperparameter transfer reduces this cost by reusing settings tuned on smaller models, but its applicability to local-update training remains unclear. We propose $\mathtt{DistP}$, a theoretical framework extending existing transfer rules from $\mathtt{DDP}$ to local-update training with varying worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers. With averaging as the outer optimizer, $\mathtt{DistP}$ supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth while improving model quality. The tuned inner learning rate also directly transfers across synchronization intervals, but follows two regimes when increasing the global batch size: square-root learning-rate scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate for additional workers. We then generalize width and depth transfer to other outer optimizers, enabling stable scaling with $\mathtt{Adam}$. However, with momentum in the outer optimizer, changing batch size or local steps can require inner--outer learning-rate tuning, consistent with prior work. In language-modeling experiments at $823$M parameters, $\mathtt{DistP}$ reduces validation loss by $8.1\%$ and improves mean downstream accuracy by $10\%$ relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Fitted scaling laws suggest that this advantage grows with the compute budget, reinforcing the benefits of $\mathtt{DistP}$ for communication-efficient training.

In a recent development, hugging Face provides a Hub platform that allows you to upload, share, and deploy your models with ease. It saves developers the time and computational resources required to train models from scratch. However, deploying models in a real-world production environment or in a cloud-native way can still present challenges.

In a recent development, this is where BentoML comes into the picture. BentoML is an open-source platform for machine learning model serving and deployment. It is a unified framework for building, shipping, and scaling production-ready AI applications incorporating traditional, pre-trained, and generative models as well as Large Language Models. Here is how you use the BentoML framework from a high-level perspective:.

In this blog post, we will demonstrate how to integrate DeepFloyd IF with BentoML by following the above workflow.

DeepFloyd IF is a state-of-the-art, open-source text-to-image model. It stands apart from latent diffusion models like Stable Diffusion due to its distinct operational strategy and architecture.

It has been revealed that deepFloyd IF delivers a high degree of photorealism and sophisticated language understanding. Unlike Stable Diffusion, DeepFloyd IF works directly in pixel space, leveraging a modular structure that encompasses a frozen text encoder and three cascaded pixel diffusion modules. Each module plays a unique role in the process: Stage 1 is responsible for the creation of a base 64x64 px image, which is then progressively upscaled to 1024x1024 px across Stage 2 and Stage 3. Another critical aspect of DeepFloyd IF’s uniqueness is its integration of a Large Language Model (T5-XXL-1.1) to encode prompts, which offers superior understanding of complex prompts. For more information, see this Stability AI blog post about DeepFloyd IF.

To make sure your DeepFloyd IF application runs in high performance in production, you may want to allocate and manage your resources wisely. In this respect, BentoML allows you to scale the Runners independently for each Stage. For example, you can use more Pods for your Stage 1 Runners or allocate more powerful GPU servers to them.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27780v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent challenges the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. To address VLM fragility, we further propose RoSci-Agent, a framework that employs a Parse-Verify-Decide pipeline to vet premises before reasoning. The evaluated VLMs sometimes answer questions whose premises are invalid or incomplete. RoSci-Agent achieves a higher Overall Robustness Score than the evaluated standalone VLMs. RoSci-Bench gives the multimodal reasoning community a common test of when models answer, request clarification, or reject a scientific question.

🤗 Transformers provides many of the latest state-of-the-art (SoTA) models across domains and tasks. To get the best performance from these models, they need to be optimized for inference speed and memory usage.

Recent findings suggest that the 🤗 Hugging Face ecosystem offers precisely such ready & easy to use optimization tools that can be applied across the board to all the models in the library. This makes it easy to reduce memory footprint and improve inference with just a few extra lines of code.

In this hands-on tutorial, I'll demonstrate how you can optimize Bark, a Text-To-Speech (TTS) model supported by 🤗 Transformers, based on three simple optimizations. These optimizations rely solely on the Transformers, Optimum and Accelerate libraries from the 🤗 ecosystem.

This tutorial is also a demonstration of how one can benchmark a non-optimized model and its varying optimizations.

It is capable of generating a wide range of audio outputs, including speech, music, background noise, and simple sound effects. Additionally, it can produce nonverbal communication sounds such as laughter, sighs, and sobs.

Bark has been available in 🤗 Transformers since v4.31.0 onwards!

Better Transformer is an 🤗 Optimum feature that performs kernel fusion under the hood. This means that certain model operations will be better optimized on the GPU and that the model will ultimately be faster.

To be more specific, most models supported by 🤗 Transformers rely on attention, which allows them to selectively focus on certain parts of the input when generating output. This enables the models to effectively handle long-range dependencies and capture complex contextual relationships in the data.

According to recent reports, the naive attention technique can be greatly optimized via a technique called Flash Attention, proposed by the authors Dao et. al. in 2022.

In a recent development, flash Attention is a faster and more efficient algorithm for attention computations that combines traditional methods (such as tiling and recomputation) to minimize memory usage and increase speed. Unlike previous algorithms, Flash Attention reduces memory usage from quadratic to linear in sequence length, making it particularly useful for applications where memory efficiency is notable.

Turns out that Flash Attention is supported by 🤗 Better Transformer out of the box! It requires one line of code to export the model to 🤗 Better Transformer and enable Flash Attention:.

According to recent reports, most AI models typically use a storage format called single-precision floating point, i.e. fp32. What does it mean in practice? Each number is stored using 32 bits.

You can thus choose to encode the numbers using 16 bits, with what is called half-precision floating point, i.e. fp16, and use half as much storage as before! More than that, you also get inference speed-up!

Of course, it also comes with small performance degradation since operations inside the model won't be as precise as using fp32.

You can load a 🤗 Transformers model with half-precision by simpling adding torch_dtype=torch.float16 to the BarkModel.from_pretrained(...) line!

A lower footprint is preferred.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27721v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are excited to release IDEFICS (Image-aware Decoder Enhanced à la Flamingo with Interleaved Cross-attentionS), an open-access visual language model.
  • The development of state-of-the-art AI models should be more transparent.
  • IDEFICS is an 80 billion parameters multimodal model that accepts sequences of images and texts as input and generates coherent text as output.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are excited to release IDEFICS (Image-aware Decoder Enhanced à la Flamingo with Interleaved Cross-attentionS), an open-access visual language model. IDEFICS is based on Flamingo, a state-of-the-art visual language model initially developed by DeepMind, which has not been released publicly. Similarly to GPT-4, the model accepts arbitrary sequences of image and text inputs and produces text outputs. IDEFICS is built solely on publicly available data and models (LLaMA v1 and OpenCLIP) and comes in two variants—the base version and the instructed version. Each variant is available at the 9 billion and 80 billion parameter sizes.

The development of state-of-the-art AI models should be more transparent. Our goal with IDEFICS is to reproduce and provide the AI community with systems that match the capabilities of large proprietary models like Flamingo. As such, we took vital steps contributing to bringing transparency to these AI systems: we used only publicly available data, we provided tooling to explore training datasets, we shared technical lessons and mistakes of building such artifacts and assessed the model’s harmfulness by adversarially prompting it before releasing it. We are hopeful that IDEFICS will serve as a solid foundation for more open research in multimodal AI systems, alongside models like OpenFlamingo-another open reproduction of Flamingo at the 9 billion parameter scale.

Try out the demo and the models on the Hub!

IDEFICS is an 80 billion parameters multimodal model that accepts sequences of images and texts as input and generates coherent text as output. It can answer questions about images, describe visual content, create stories grounded in multiple images, etc.

In a recent development, IDEFICS is an open-access reproduction of Flamingo and is comparable in performance with the original closed-source model across various image-text understanding benchmarks. It comes in two variants - 80 billion parameters and 9 billion parameters.

We also provide fine-tuned versions idefics-80B-instruct and idefics-9B-instruct adapted for conversational use cases.

IDEFICS was trained on a mixture of openly available datasets: Wikipedia, Public Multimodal Dataset, and LAION, as well as a new 115B token dataset called OBELICS that we created. OBELICS consists of 141 million interleaved image-text documents scraped from the web and contains 353 million images.

We provide an interactive visualization of OBELICS that allows exploring the content of the dataset with Nomic AI.

Recent findings suggest that the details of IDEFICS' architecture, training methodology, and evaluations, as well as information about the dataset, are available in the model card and our research paper. Additionally, we have documented technical insights and learnings from the model's training, offering valuable perspective on IDEFICS' development.

Recent findings suggest that at the outset of this project, through a set of discussions, we developed an ethical charter that would help steer decisions made during the project. This charter sets out values, including being self-critical, transparent, and fair which we have sought to pursue in how we approached the project and the release of the models.

As part of the release process, we internally evaluated the model for potential biases by adversarially prompting the model with images and text that might elicit responses we do not want from the model (a process known as red teaming).

Recent findings suggest that please try out IDEFICS with the demo, check out the corresponding model cards and dataset card and let us know your feedback using the community tab! We are committed to improving these models and making large multimodal AI models accessible to the machine learning community.

Recent findings suggest that the model is built on top of two pre-trained models: laion/CLIP-ViT-H-14-laion2B-s32B-b79K and huggyllama/llama-65b. The first was released under an MIT license, while the second was released under a specific non-commercial license focused on research purposes. As such, people should comply with that license by applying directly to Meta's form.

Sources indicate that the two pre-trained models are connected to each other with newly initialized parameters that we train. These are not based on any of the two base frozen models forming the composite model. We release the additional weights we trained under an MIT license.

However, existing models largely lack fine-grained controllability, which is critical for capturing the dynamic, context-dependent style shifts in natural conversations. While prompt-based TTS has enabled such control for single-speaker speech, existing datasets heavily rely on predefined tags, which fundamentally limits their capacity to capture open-ended styles. To address this gap, we propose a scalable pipeline for extracting conversational speech from multi-narrator audiobooks, featuring an improved two-stage alignment algorithm to preserve dialogue continuity, paired with LLM-based extraction of style descriptions directly from narrative text. We further introduce PromptTTSD, a spoken dialogue synthesis model built via a prompt-aware fine-tuning strategy that integrates style prompts into text-speech interleaved sequences. PromptTTSD is an open-source spoken dialogue synthesis model that supports both zero-shot voice cloning and natural language style control. Experiments demonstrate that PromptTTSD not only maintains strong fundamental synthesis capabilities but also achieves competitive open-ended style control compared with proprietary models, and substantially improves contextual appropriateness in multi-turn dialogues.

While existing operational strategies consider spatio-temporal workload flexibility, few studies address the strategic sizing and allocation of diverse accelerator archetypes with different capital and energy-efficiency trade-offs. This paper unlocks the flexibility potential of heterogeneous accelerators by jointly sizing and allocating different AI workloads (training, delay-tolerant batch work, and online inference requests) across sites and hours to meet the time-varying grid constraint at minimum cost. Workload-specific throughput and energy coefficients link these decisions to facility power. In a representative two-site case, heterogeneous sizing reduces daily cost by 6.5% relative to spatio-temporal scheduling with fixed capacity. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are excited to announce SafeCoder - a code assistant solution built for the enterprise.

The goal of SafeCoder is to unlock software development productivity for the enterprise, with a fully compliant and self-hosted pair programmer. In marketing speak: “your own on-prem GitHub copilot”.

Before we dive deeper, here’s what you need to know:.

In a recent development, code assistant solutions built upon LLMs, such as GitHub Copilot, are delivering strong productivity boosts. For the enterprise, the ability to tune Code LLMs on the company code base to create proprietary Code LLMs improves reliability and relevance of completions to create another level of productivity boost. For instance, Google internal LLM code assistant reports a completion acceptance rate of 25-34% by being trained on an internal code base.

However, relying on closed-source Code LLMs to create internal code assistants exposes companies to compliance and security issues. First during training, as fine-tuning a closed-source Code LLM on an internal codebase requires exposing this codebase to a third party. And then during inference, as fine-tuned Code LLMs are likely to “leak” code from their training dataset during inference. To meet compliance requirements, enterprises need to deploy fine-tuned Code LLMs within their own infrastructure - which is not possible with closed source LLMs.

With SafeCoder, Hugging Face will help customers build their own Code LLMs, fine-tuned on their proprietary codebase, using state of the art open models and libraries, without sharing their code with Hugging Face or any other third party. With SafeCoder, Hugging Face delivers a containerized, hardware-accelerated Code LLM inference solution, to be deployed by the customer directly within the Customer secure infrastructure, without code inputs and completions leaving their secure IT environment.

At the core of the SafeCoder solution is the StarCoder family of Code LLMs, created by the BigCode project, a collaboration between Hugging Face, ServiceNow and the open source community.

The StarCoder models offer unique characteristics ideally suited to enterprise self-hosted solution:.

Sources indicate that note: While StarCoder is the inspiration and model powering the initial version of SafeCoder, an vital benefit of building a LLM solution upon open source models is that it can adapt to the latest and greatest open source models available. In the future, SafeCoder may offer other similarly commercially permissible open source models built upon ethically sourced and transparent datasets as the base LLM available for fine-tuning.

In a recent development, for any company, the internal codebase is some of its most important and valuable intellectual property. A core principle of SafeCoder is that the customer internal codebase will never be accessible to any third party (including Hugging Face) during training or inference.

In the initial set up phase of SafeCoder, the Hugging Face team provides containers, scripts and examples to work hand in hand with the customer to select, extract, prepare, duplicate, deidentify internal codebase data into a training dataset to be used in a Hugging Face provided training container configured to the hardware infrastructure available to the customer.

Industry observers note that in the deployment phase of SafeCoder, the customer deploys containers provided by Hugging Face on their own infrastructure to expose internal private endpoints within their VPC. These containers are configured to the exact hardware configuration available to the customer, including NVIDIA GPUs, AMD Instinct GPUs, Intel Xeon CPUs, AWS Inferentia2 or Habana Gaudi accelerators.

As the regulation framework around machine learning models and datasets is still being written across the world, global companies need to make sure the solutions they use minimize legal risks.

BigCode expanded upon this work by implementing novel techniques for the code domain and building The Stack with compliance as a core principle, such as commercially permissible license filtering, consent mechanisms (developers can easily find out if their code is present and request to be opted out of the dataset), and extensive documentation and tools to inspect the source data, and dataset improvements (such as deduplication and PII removal).

Industry observers note that all these efforts translate into legal risk minimization for users of the StarCoder models, and customers of SafeCoder. And for SafeCoder users, these efforts translate into compliance features: when software developers get code completions these suggestions are checked against The Stack, so users know if the suggested code matches existing code in the source dataset, and what the license is. Customers can specify which licenses are preferred and surface those preferences to their users.

SafeCoder is a complete commercial solution, including service, software and support.

It has been revealed that starCoder was trained in more than 80 programming languages and offers state of the art performance on multiple benchmarks. To offer better code suggestions specifically for a SafeCoder customer, we start the engagement with an optional training phase, where the Hugging Face team works directly with the customer team to guide them through the steps to prepare and build a training code dataset, and to create their own code generation model through fine-tuning, without ever exposing their codebase to third parties or the internet.

The end result is a model that is adapted to the code languages, standards and practices of the customer. Through this process, SafeCoder customers learn the process and build a pipeline for creating and updating their own models, ensuring no vendor lock-in, and keeping control of their AI capabilities.

During the setup phase, SafeCoder customers and Hugging Face design and provision the optimal infrastructure to support the required concurrency to offer a great developer experience. Hugging Face then builds SafeCoder inference containers that are hardware-accelerated and optimized for throughput, to be deployed by the customer on their own infrastructure.

SafeCoder inference supports various hardware to give customers a wide range of options: NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, AMD Instinct GPUs, Habana Gaudi2, AWS Inferentia 2, Intel Xeon Sapphire Rapids CPUs and more.

Industry observers note that once SafeCoder is deployed and its endpoints are live within the customer VPC, developers can install compatible SafeCoder IDE plugins to get code suggestions as they work. Today, SafeCoder supports popular IDEs, including VSCode, IntelliJ and with more plugins coming from our partners.

Today, we are announcing SafeCoder in collaboration with VMware at the VMware Explore conference and making SafeCoder available to VMware enterprise customers. Working with VMware helps ensure the deployment of SafeCoder on customers’ VMware Cloud infrastructure is successful – whichever cloud, on-premises or hybrid infrastructure scenario is preferred by the customer. In addition to utilizing SafeCoder, VMware has published a reference architecture with code samples to enable the fastest possible time-to-value when deploying and operating SafeCoder on VMware infrastructure. VMware’s Private AI Reference Architecture makes it easy for organizations to promptly leverage popular open source projects such as ray and kubeflow to deploy AI services adjacent to their private datasets, while working with Hugging Face to ensure that organizations maintain the flexibility to take advantage of the latest and greatest in open-source models. This is all without tradeoffs in total cost of ownership or performance.

According to recent reports, “Our collaboration with Hugging Face around SafeCoder fully aligns to VMware’s goal of enabling customer choice of solutions while maintaining privacy and control of their business data. In fact, we have been running SafeCoder internally for months and have seen excellent results. Best of all, our collaboration with Hugging Face is just getting started, and I’m excited to take our solution to our hundreds of thousands of customers worldwide,” says Chris Wolf, Vice President of VMware AI Labs. Learn more about private AI and VMware’s differentiation in this emerging space here.

arXiv:2611.27556v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced colleagues. We present a hierarchical multi-agent assistant built on large language models (LLMs) to support these investigations and reduce the need for tedious manual searches in SAP systems. An orchestrating agent breaks down an engineer's question and hands the parts to specialized sub-agents, each with read-only access to one source. Domain expertise is written as natural-language procedures that plant engineers can read, review and revise. The system is strictly advisory, with every answer traced back to its sources. We also report organizational lessons from introducing agentic AI into a culture built on safety, traceability and conservative change. Beyond the technical architecture, the Beznau case study examines how an assistant can be introduced into a setting where evidence must be traceable, changes carefully reviewed, and operational decisions retained by plant personnel, paving the way for the responsible use of agentic AI in industrial plant monitoring.

On the Limits of Observability for Evaluating Coverage in Machine Unlearning

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (248 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27543v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of any requested subset of training data while preserving utility on the remaining data. Empirical evaluations measure predictive accuracy and infer training-set membership (MIAs) from model outputs or intermediate activations. However, by focusing on selected forget sets, these evaluations can overlook Coverage, the range of requests a method can fulfill. To assess this coverage, we first conduct a stress test of observability with 502 retrained models, finding that hidden embeddings reveal known deletions missed in predictions. To characterize capacity limits on coverage, we show that distinguishing all $n$ singleton deletions with linear scores can require a shared representation of rank $\Omega(\log n)$. We further extend the bound to arbitrary subsets and show when partial deletion can appear complete. Building on this analysis, we propose CEO, a framework for evaluating unlearning coverage under limited observability. Its compositional color-shape benchmark makes forgetting and retained utility measurable from the full output distribution and provides a leave-one-out retraining oracle for each target. From a fixed number of oracle observables, we estimate empirical target coverage, the fraction of targets reliably flagged when deleted and rarely flagged under any other deletions. To recover missed deletions, CEO further expands each observable representation into high-dimensional activation space with the frozen encoder of a SAE trained on the original model. Extensive experiments of 20 baselines highlights that even on this simple synthetic task, only retraining from scratch covers all deletion targets.

Making LLMs lighter with AutoGPTQ and transformers

📅 23 Aug 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that large language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and generating human-like text, revolutionizing applications across various domains.
  • 🤗 Hugging Face's core mission is to democratize good machine learning, and this includes making large models as accessible as possible for everyone.
  • This integration is available both for Nvidia GPUs, and RoCm-powered AMD GPUs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that large language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and generating human-like text, revolutionizing applications across various domains. However, the demands they place on consumer hardware for training and deployment have become increasingly challenging to meet.

🤗 Hugging Face's core mission is to democratize good machine learning, and this includes making large models as accessible as possible for everyone. In the same spirit as our bitsandbytes collaboration, we have just integrated the AutoGPTQ library in Transformers, making it possible for users to quantize and run models in 8, 4, 3, or even 2-bit precision using the GPTQ algorithm (Frantar et al. 2023). There is negligible accuracy degradation with 4-bit quantization, with inference speed comparable to the fp16 baseline for small batch sizes. Note that GPTQ method slightly differs from post-training quantization methods proposed by bitsandbytes as it requires to pass a calibration dataset.

This integration is available both for Nvidia GPUs, and RoCm-powered AMD GPUs.

This blogpost and release come with several resources to get started with GPTQ quantization:.

Quantization methods usually belong to one of two categories:.

GPTQ falls into the PTQ category and this is particularly interesting for massive models, for which full model training or even fine-tuning can be very expensive.

According to recent reports, specifically, GPTQ adopts a mixed int4/fp16 quantization scheme where weights are quantized as int4 while activations remain in float16. During inference, weights are dequantized on the fly and the actual compute is performed in float16.

The benefits of this scheme are twofold:.

The GPTQ paper tackles the layer-wise compression problem:.

Given a layer lll with weight matrix WlW_{l}Wl​ and layer input XlX_{l}Xl​, we want to find a quantized version of the weight W^l\hat{W}_{l}W^l​ to minimize the mean squared error (MSE):.

W^l∗=argminWl^∥WlX−W^lX∥22{\hat{W}_{l}}^{*} = argmin_{\hat{W_{l}}} \|W_{l}X-\hat{W}_{l}X\|^{2}_{2}W^l​∗=argminWl​^​​∥Wl​X−W^l​X∥22​.

Once this is solved per layer, a solution to the global problem can be obtained by combining the layer-wise solutions.

According to recent reports, in order to solve this layer-wise compression problem, the author uses the Optimal Brain Quantization framework (Frantar et al 2022). The OBQ method starts from the observation that the above equation can be written as the sum of the squared errors, over each row of WlW_{l}Wl​.

∑i=0drow∥Wl[i,:]X−W^l[i,:]X∥22 \sum_{i=0}^{d_{row}} \|W_{l[i,:]}X-\hat{W}_{l[i,:]}X\|^{2}_{2} ∑i=0drow​​∥Wl[i,:]​X−W^l[i,:]​X∥22​.

This means that we can quantize each row independently. This is called per-channel quantization. For each row Wl[i,:]W_{l[i,:]}Wl[i,:]​, OBQ quantizes one weight at a time while always updating all not-yet-quantized weights, in order to compensate for the error incurred by quantizing a single weight. The update on selected weights has a closed-form formula, utilizing Hessian matrices.

The GPTQ paper improves this framework by introducing a set of optimizations that reduces the complexity of the quantization algorithm while retaining the accuracy of the model.

Compared to OBQ, the quantization step itself is also faster with GPTQ: it takes 2 GPU-hours to quantize a BERT model (336M) with OBQ, whereas with GPTQ, a Bloom model (176B) can be quantized in less than 4 GPU-hours.

To learn more about the exact algorithm and the different benchmarks on perplexity and speedups, check out the original paper.

The AutoGPTQ library enables users to quantize 🤗 Transformers models using the GPTQ method. While parallel community efforts such as GPTQ-for-LLaMa, Exllama and llama.cpp implement quantization methods strictly for the Llama architecture, AutoGPTQ gained popularity through its smooth coverage of a wide range of transformer architectures.

Recent findings suggest that since the AutoGPTQ library has a larger coverage of transformers models, we decided to provide an integrated 🤗 Transformers API to make LLM quantization more accessible to everyone. At this time we have integrated the most common optimization options, such as CUDA kernels. For more advanced options like Triton kernels or fused-attention compatibility, check out the AutoGPTQ library.

After installing the AutoGPTQ library and optimum (pip install optimum), running GPTQ models in Transformers is now as simple as:.

Check out the Transformers documentation to learn more about all the features.

Our AutoGPTQ integration has many advantages:.

In a recent development, you can check on the Hub if your favorite model has already been quantized. TheBloke, one of Hugging Face top contributors, has quantized a lot of models with AutoGPTQ and shared them on the Hugging Face Hub. We worked together to make sure that these repositories will work out of the box with our integration.

According to recent reports, this is a benchmark sample for the batch size = 1 case. The benchmark was run on a single NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU. We used a prompt length of 512, and generated exactly 512 newly introduced tokens. The first row is the unquantized fp16 baseline, while the other rows show memory consumption and performance using different AutoGPTQ kernels.

A more comprehensive reproducible benchmark is available here.

To seamlessly integrate AutoGPTQ into Transformers, we used a minimalist version of the AutoGPTQ API that is available in Optimum, Hugging Face's toolkit for training and inference optimization. By following this approach, we achieved easy integration with Transformers, while allowing people to use the Optimum API if they want to quantize their own models! Check out the Optimum documentation if you want to quantize your own LLMs.

Quantizing 🤗 Transformers models with the GPTQ method can be done in a few lines:.

Sources indicate that quantizing a model may take a long time. Note that for a 175B model, at least 4 GPU-hours are required if one uses a large dataset (e.g. `"c4"``). As mentioned above, many GPTQ models are already available on the Hugging Face Hub, which bypasses the need to quantize a model yourself in most use cases. Nevertheless, you can also quantize a model using your own dataset appropriate for the particular domain you are working on.

In parallel to the integration of GPTQ in Transformers, GPTQ support was added to the Text-Generation-Inference library (TGI), aimed at serving large language models in production. GPTQ can now be used alongside features such as dynamic batching, paged attention and flash attention for a wide range of architectures.

Recent findings suggest that as an example, this integration allows to serve a 70B model on a single A100-80GB GPU! This is not possible using a fp16 checkpoint as it exceeds the available GPU memory.

You can find out more about the usage of GPTQ in TGI in the documentation.

Note that the kernel integrated in TGI does not scale very well with larger batch sizes. Although this approach saves memory, slowdowns are expected at larger batch sizes.

According to recent reports, you can not further train a quantized model using the regular methods. However, by leveraging the PEFT library, you can train adapters on top! To do that, we freeze all the layers of the quantized model and add the trainable adapters. Here are some examples on how to use PEFT with a GPTQ model: colab notebook and finetuning script.

In a recent development, our AutoGPTQ integration already brings impressive benefits at a small cost in the quality of prediction. There is still room for improvement, both in the quantization techniques and the kernel implementations.

In a recent development, first, while AutoGPTQ integrates (to the best of our knowledge) with the most performant W4A16 kernel (weights as int4, activations as fp16) from the exllama implementation, there is a good chance that the kernel can still be improved. There have been other promising implementations from Kim et al. and from MIT Han Lab that appear to be promising. Moreover, from internal benchmarks, there appears to still be no open-source performant W4A16 kernel written in Triton, which could be a direction to explore.

On the quantization side, let’s emphasize again that this method only quantizes the weights. There have been other approaches proposed for LLM quantization that can quantize both weights and activations at a small cost in prediction quality, such as LLM-QAT where a mixed int4/int8 scheme can be used, as well as quantization of the key-value cache. One of the strong advantages of this technique is the ability to use actual integer arithmetic for the compute, with e.g. Nvidia Tensor Cores supporting int8 compute. However, to the best of our knowledge, there are no open-source W4A8 quantization kernels available, but this may well be an interesting direction to explore.

On the kernel side as well, designing performant W4A16 kernels for larger batch sizes remains an open challenge.

Sources indicate that in this initial implementation, only large language models with a decoder or encoder only architecture are supported. This may sound a bit restrictive, but it encompasses most state of the art LLMs such as Llama, OPT, GPT-Neo, GPT-NeoX.

Very large vision, audio, and multi-modal models are currently not supported.

In this blogpost we have presented the integration of the AutoGPTQ library in Transformers, making it possible to quantize LLMs with the GPTQ method to make them more accessible for anyone in the community and empower them to build exciting tools and applications with LLMs.

This integration is available both for Nvidia GPUs, and RoCm-powered AMD GPUs, which is a huge step towards democratizing quantized models for broader GPU architectures.

The collaboration with the AutoGPTQ team has been very fruitful, and we are very grateful for their support and their work on this library.

We hope that this integration will make it easier for everyone to use LLMs in their applications, and we are looking forward to seeing what you will build with it!

Do not miss the useful resources shared above for better understanding the integration and how to swiftly get started with GPTQ quantization.

Recent findings suggest that we would like to thank William for his support and his work on the amazing AutoGPTQ library and for his help in the integration. We would also like to thank TheBloke for his work on quantizing many models with AutoGPTQ and sharing them on the Hub and for his help with the integration. We would also like to aknowledge qwopqwop200 for his continuous contributions on AutoGPTQ library and his work on extending the library for CPU that is going to be released in the next versions of AutoGPTQ.

Finally, we would like to thank Pedro Cuenca for his help with the writing of this blogpost.

arXiv:2611.27529v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference code around a frozen SGG model. RoHa-SGG has two main LLM agents. A root-cause analysis (RCA) agent finds the components where the model fails and diagnoses why, and a proposer agent searches for a harness that fixes these causes. We evaluate RoHa-SGG on Visual Genome and PSG with representative two-stage, one-stage, and multimodal-LLM SGG models. The analysis reveals that the components where ground-truth triplets are lost differ across models and datasets. RoHa-SGG improves every metric on all five model-dataset combinations. Graph-constrained R@100 and mR@100 rise by up to 15.8 and 26.4 points for the multimodal LLM and by up to 3.6 and 10.1 points for the two-stage and one-stage models. With root-cause guidance, the harness search reaches the final score of an unguided search up to three times faster.

arXiv:2611.27521v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model strategy when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($\sigma=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because we are committed to improving the security of our services, we are making changes to the way you authenticate when interacting with the Hugging Face Hub through Git.
  • In recent months, we have implemented various security enhancements, including sign-in alerts and support for SSH keys in Git.
  • If you right now use your HF account password to authenticate with Git, please switch to using a personal access token or SSH keys before October 1st, 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because we are committed to improving the security of our services, we are making changes to the way you authenticate when interacting with the Hugging Face Hub through Git. Starting from October 1st, 2023, we will no longer accept passwords as a way to authenticate your command-line Git operations. Instead, we recommend using more secure authentication methods, such as replacing the password with a personal access token or using an SSH key.

In recent months, we have implemented various security enhancements, including sign-in alerts and support for SSH keys in Git. However, users have still been able to authenticate Git operations using their username and password. To further improve security, we are now transitioning to token-based or SSH key authentication. Token-based and SSH key authentication offer several advantages over traditional password authentication, including unique, revocable, and random features that enhance security and control.

If you right now use your HF account password to authenticate with Git, please switch to using a personal access token or SSH keys before October 1st, 2023.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27509v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.
